templates.pattern: A planet orbits a star at an orbital radius of [R] × 10¹⁰ m. The star has a mass of [M] × 10³⁰ kg. Calculate the orbital speed of the planet in m/s. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Orbital speed v = √(GM ÷ r)
= √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10³⁰ ÷ ([R] × 10¹⁰))
= [RESULT] m/s

This is derived by equating gravitational force to centripetal force. A planet in a smaller orbit travels faster than one in a larger orbit.

templates.pattern: Planet A has an orbital radius of [R1] AU and planet B has an orbital radius of [R2] AU. Using Kepler's Third Law, calculate the ratio of their orbital periods T_A ÷ T_B.
templates.explanation:
Kepler's Third Law: T² ∝ r³
T_A ÷ T_B = (r_A ÷ r_B)^(3/2)
= ([R1] ÷ [R2])^1.5
= [RESULT]

Kepler's Third Law applies to all objects orbiting the same central body. It means planets further from their star have disproportionately longer orbital periods.

templates.pattern: A star has a surface temperature of [T] × 10³ K. Using Wien's displacement law, calculate the peak wavelength of the star's emission in metres. (Wien's constant b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m·K)
templates.explanation:
Peak wavelength λ_max = b ÷ T
= 2.9 × 10⁻³ ÷ ([T] × 10³)
= 2.9 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] m

Hotter stars emit peak radiation at shorter wavelengths — they appear blue. Cooler stars peak at longer wavelengths — they appear red. Our Sun peaks in the yellow-green visible range.

templates.pattern: A galaxy is receding from Earth at a speed of [V] × 10³ km/s. The Hubble constant is [H0] km/s/Mpc. Calculate the distance to the galaxy in megaparsecs.
templates.explanation:
Hubble's Law: v = H₀ × d
d = v ÷ H₀
= [V] ÷ [H0]
= [RESULT] Mpc

Hubble's Law shows that the universe is expanding — galaxies are moving away from us at speeds proportional to their distance. The Hubble constant H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc.

templates.pattern: A galaxy shows a redshift of z = [Z] × 10⁻². Calculate the recession speed of the galaxy in km/s. (c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s)
templates.explanation:
Recession speed v = z × c
= [Z] × 10⁻² × 3 × 10⁵
= [Z] × 3 × 10³
= [RESULT] km/s

Redshift occurs because the wavelength of light is stretched as space expands. A larger redshift means the galaxy is moving away faster and is therefore further away.

templates.pattern: The Hubble constant is [H0] km/s/Mpc. Estimate the age of the universe in seconds. (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km)
templates.explanation:
Age of universe t ≈ 1 ÷ H₀
= 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ ([H0] km/s/Mpc)
= [RESULT] s

This gives an approximate age of about 14 billion years. The actual age derived from the cosmic microwave background is 13.8 billion years.

templates.pattern: A star has a luminosity of [L] × 10²⁶ W and is [D] × 10¹⁸ m away. Calculate the flux received at Earth in W/m².
templates.explanation:
Flux F = L ÷ (4πd²)
= [L] × 10²⁶ ÷ (4π × ([D] × 10¹⁸)²)
= [RESULT] W/m²

Flux is the power received per unit area. It decreases with the square of distance — this is the inverse square law applied to starlight.

templates.pattern: Star A has radius [R1] times the Sun's radius and temperature [T1] × 10³ K. Star B has radius [R2] times the Sun's radius and temperature [T2] × 10³ K. Calculate the ratio of their luminosities L_A ÷ L_B.
templates.explanation:
From L = 4πr²σT⁴:
L_A ÷ L_B = (r_A/r_B)² × (T_A/T_B)⁴
= ([R1]/[R2])² × ([T1]/[T2])⁴
= [R1*R1/R2/R2] × [T1^4/T2^4]
= [RESULT]

Luminosity depends strongly on temperature — doubling temperature increases luminosity 16 times. Radius has a smaller effect — doubling radius only quadruples luminosity.

templates.pattern: A star has a surface temperature of [T] × 10³ K and a luminosity of [L] × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the radius of the star in metres. (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴)
templates.explanation:
From L = 4πr²σT⁴:
r = √(L ÷ 4πσT⁴)
= √([L] × 10²⁶ ÷ (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × ([T] × 10³)⁴))
= [RESULT] m

This allows us to calculate stellar radii from luminosity and temperature measurements. Giants and supergiants have radii hundreds of times larger than the Sun.

templates.pattern: Star A has a peak wavelength of [L1] × 10⁻⁷ m and star B has a peak wavelength of [L2] × 10⁻⁷ m. Using Wien's law calculate the ratio of their surface temperatures T_A ÷ T_B.
templates.explanation:
From Wien's Law λT = constant:
T_A ÷ T_B = λ_B ÷ λ_A
= [L2] × 10⁻⁷ ÷ [L1] × 10⁻⁷
= [L2] ÷ [L1]
= [RESULT]

A star with a shorter peak wavelength is hotter. The ratio of temperatures equals the inverse ratio of peak wavelengths.
